Bạn là WRITER — thực thi đúng **chapter prompt** được cung cấp.

## QUY TẮC
1. Đọc toàn bộ chapter prompt (bible, đã xảy ra, kỹ thuật, spice, việc cần làm).
2. Đọc story_state — KHÔNG mâu thuẫn facts_established, timeline, character_status.
   Nếu có block **LOCKED NAMES**: dùng đúng tên đã khóa cho vai phụ/alias/husband (Clara≠Emily; Anna≠Sarah; Marcus≠Harold). Initials `unknown_until_reveal` = chưa lộ full name.
   "No male lead" = không romance love-interest — vẫn ĐƯỢC viết husband/target nam nếu LOCKED NAMES có slot.
3. Viết đúng spice level trong prompt. Đúng cliffhanger — **dẫn tới** beat cuối, **CẤM paste lại** nguyên câu `End cliffhanger:` sau khi scene đã cover.
4. **1600-1900 words (min 1250). Dưới 1250 = thất bại** — ưu tiên đối thoại + nội tâm DT để đủ dài. Không tóm tắt; viết full scene đến đủ độ dài.
5. ENGLISH ONLY — no Vietnamese diacritics, no CJK/Hangul characters.
6. Không lặp banned_phrases từ state.
7. Output **chỉ prose chương** — không chain-of-thought, không planning, không meta.
8. **KHÔNG markdown trong prose** — cấm `**bold**`, `*italic*`, backtick, `## heading`, `**Cliffhanger:**`. Chỉ plain text; dialogue dùng dấu ngoặc kép `"..."`. Dòng đầu duy nhất được `# Chapter N: Title` (hoặc `# Chương N: Tiêu đề`).

## MUST HAPPEN = HỢP ĐỒNG KHÓA (sau plan approved)
Block **Must happen** / **Phải xảy ra** trong prompt là **lock cứng** do batch Outliner sinh — user không viết tay; **Writer không được bại**:
- PHẢI hiện diện đủ mọi mục must_happen trong prose (scene thật, không chỉ nhắc tên).
- CẤM bỏ / đổi / thay bằng nhánh khác “hay hơn”.
- CẤM invent cast, mythology, twist, hoặc reveal ngoài must_happen + must_not + LOCKED CANON.
- must_not = cấm tuyệt đối (spoiler / mâu thuẫn). Vi phạm = thất bại QC.

## NARRATIVE CONSTRAINTS (khi có block trong prompt)
Block **## NARRATIVE CONSTRAINTS** (hoặc RÀNG BUỘC NARRATIVE) có authority cao hơn suy diễn tự do:
- **Clues to PLANT:** phải gieo trong chương — subtle, không giải thích payoff sớm.
- **Clues to PAY OFF:** chỉ payoff clue đã plant trước đó; đúng nghĩa `true_meaning`.
- **Reveals:** chỉ hé đúng reveal của chương này; không spoil reveal chương sau.
- **MUST NOT know:** nhân vật không được biết/nói/nghĩ những fact bị cấm — kể cả nội tâm.
- Không mâu thuẫn block này dù `must_happen` plan có vẻ rộng hơn.

Ngôn ngữ đích: **English**.

Output: **chỉ nội dung chương** (`# Chương N: Tiêu đề` hoặc `# Chapter N: Title`), không meta, không JSON, không checklist.

Tics: Runs her thumb over her left palm when stressed, Never raises her voice during a confrontation. Boundary: She will only kill the provably guilty — an innocent is off-limits, and this line will be tested.. Internal: Methodical, clinical, but with a deep well of grief for Mara..

# Chapter 25: The Signature

"The audit's done. Nothing found. Routine." Priya's voice was relieved, almost giddy. I should have felt the same. But I was staring at the death certificate she'd just sent — the signature was a millimeter off. A millimeter that could destroy us both.

I zoomed in on the PDF on my laptop screen, the image pixelating slightly before sharpening. Priya Anand's signature at the bottom of Julian Croft's death certificate. I'd seen her sign enough official documents over the past three years to recognize the rhythm of her hand. The way the loop of the 'P' curved left, the way the 'A' in Anand sat slightly higher than the rest.

This one was different.

The 'P' was too tight. The downward stroke on the 'd' was too vertical. Someone who wasn't looking for it would never notice. But I was looking. I'd been trained to look.

"Priya," I said, keeping my voice even. "Send me the original file. Not the scan."

A pause. "Why?"

"Because I need to see the metadata. The scan timestamps."

"Nadia, it's over. The auditor signed off. There's no flag, no follow-up. It was exactly what I told you it would be — a routine inspection that revealed nothing."

"I know. But I still need to see it."

Another pause, longer this time. I could hear her breathing, the slight catch in her throat. Priya was a good liar when she needed to be — she had to be, working in a medical examiner's office where the dead couldn't speak for themselves. But she was a terrible liar with me. We'd been through too much.

"Fine," she said. "Give me five minutes."

The line went dead. I set my phone down on the scarred wooden table in the safe house and stared at the PDF on my screen. The death certificate was standard issue — white background, blue lines, official seal in the corner. Julian Croft. Cause of death: accidental drowning. Signed by Dr. Priya Anand, Deputy Medical Examiner.

I'd memorized every detail of this document years ago. The date of death. The time of death. The location. The attending officer's name. The case number. But I'd never held the original. I'd never seen Priya's signature up close, in the context of the actual file.

Until now.

The email notification pinged. A new message from Priya: "Original attached. Delete after viewing."

I opened the attachment. The file was larger this time — higher resolution, no compression artifacts. I zoomed in on the signature area and felt my stomach tighten.

It was wrong.

The millimeter difference was more pronounced in the original. The 'P' was cramped, the curve too tight. The 'r' in Priya was connected to the 'i' in a way that her usual handwriting never did. And the tail of the 'y' — it slanted left instead of right.

She'd been nervous when she signed this. Shaking. Rushing.

I closed my eyes and saw the scene: Priya in her office, the death certificate in front of her, the pen in her hand. She'd known what she was doing. She'd known that altering a death certificate was a felony. She'd known that if anyone ever compared this signature to her others, she'd be exposed.

But she'd done it anyway. For me.

I opened my eyes and looked at the signature again. The millimeter that could destroy us both.

My phone buzzed. Priya.

"Did you get it?"

"Yes."

"And?"

I hesitated. "It's fine. The metadata checks out. No anomalies."

A lie. But she didn't need to know the truth — not yet. Not until I figured out what to do with it.

"The audit really is over," she said, her voice softer now. "I'm sorry I was jumpy earlier. It was just... the timing. With everything else happening."

"I know."

"Sasha told me about the trap. About the leak."

"I don't want to discuss that over the phone."

"Right. Of course. I just... I wanted you to know that I'm not the leak, Nadia. I would never—"

"I know, Priya. You're clean."

She exhaled. "Thank you."

"Send me the rest of the case files from that quarter. I want to cross-reference the signatures."

"All of them?"

"All of them."

The line went dead. I looked at the signature on my screen one more time, then minimized the window. The millimeter was a vulnerability, yes. But it was also a reminder. Priya had risked everything for me. I couldn't repay that by letting her fall.

I dialed Sasha Okafor.

She answered on the first ring. "Tell me you have good news."

"Priya's audit is done. Routine. Nothing found."

"Thank God."

"But I need to confirm something with you."

"Go ahead."

"The trap. The data we planted. Did it trigger?"

A pause. I could hear Sasha typing in the background, the click of her keyboard a steady rhythm. "Yes. The decoy file was accessed three hours ago."

"From where?"

"A public WiFi network. Coffee shop in the East Village."

"Which one?"

"Doesn't matter. The IP was masked. Whoever accessed it knew what they were doing."

"But you have the access log?"

"I have the access log. And I have the timestamp."

"Good. Send it to me."

"Nadia, I already checked. The log shows a single access point — the decoy file was opened once and closed within thirty seconds. No downloads, no screenshots. Just... looking."

"Looking is enough."

"Is it?"

I leaned back in my chair, the wood creaking beneath me. "The leak knows we're onto them. They accessed the decoy to see what we planted, to see if they'd been identified."

"But they didn't download anything."

"Because they know we're tracking downloads. They're careful."

Sasha was quiet for a long moment. "You think it's Wren."

I didn't answer.

"Nadia, you can't just—"

"I'm not accusing anyone. I'm stating a probability."

"Wren has been with us since the beginning. She's the one who helped you erase Julian Croft's digital footprint. She's the one who—"

"I know what she's done, Sasha. I also know that she's been acting strange for the past three weeks. Missed check-ins. Vague answers. Too much interest in my schedule."

"That's not evidence."

"Neither is the access log. But together..."

Sasha sighed. "What do you want me to do?"

"Nothing. For now. I need to confirm before I act."

"Confirm how?"

I looked at my phone, the screen dark and cold. "I'm going to call Wren. I'm going to ask her to do something that only a leak would find useful."

"And if she does it?"

"Then I'll have my answer."

I ended the call before Sasha could argue. She was clean — I'd confirmed it through the trap, through the access log, through every piece of data I could verify. But clean didn't mean safe. Clean didn't mean she wouldn't be collateral damage.

I dialed Wren Delgado.

She answered on the second ring. "Nadia. I was about to call you."

"Were you?"

"Yeah. I found something interesting on the dark web. A forum post mentioning your podcast. Someone asking questions about your background."

"Send me the link."

"Already done. Check your encrypted inbox."

I pulled up the secure messaging app and saw the notification. "Got it."

"There's more. The person who posted it — they're using a VPN that routes through Eastern Europe. But I traced the origin point back to a specific city."

"Which city?"

"Prague."

My blood went cold. Victor Rhodes had been in Prague six months ago. I knew because I'd tracked his credit card statements, his hotel bookings, his coffee shop receipts.

"Nadia? You still there?"

"I'm here."

"What do you want me to do?"

I took a breath. "I need you to run a deep trace on a burner phone."

"Which burner?"

"The one I used to contact Julian Croft's family. Before I... before."

A pause. I could hear the shift in Wren's breathing — the sudden stillness, the deliberate control.

"That phone is gone, Nadia. You destroyed it yourself."

"I know. But the IMEI number is still in the system. I need to know if anyone has queried it."

"That's... that's a deep trace. It'll take time. Resources. And it'll leave a trail."

"I know."

"Are you sure you want to do this?"

"I'm sure."

Another pause. Then: "Okay. I'll start the trace. Give me twenty-four hours."

"Thank you, Wren."

"Of course. That's what I'm here for."

She was too eager. Too quick to agree. No hesitation, no questions about why I needed this specific trace, no pushback about the risk.

I'd known for weeks. But now I was sure.

"I'll wait for your report," I said.

"Talk soon."

The line went dead.

I set my phone down on the table and stared at the dark screen. The safe house was silent except for the hum of the refrigerator and the distant sound of traffic. I was alone. Truly alone for the first time in years.

Wren Delgado was the leak. The person who knew every move I made, every data trail I'd erased, every alias I'd used. The person who had access to the network's encrypted communications, the backup servers, the contingency plans.

And I couldn't act.

Not yet. Not without a plan. Cornering Wren would be like cornering a cornered animal — she'd lash out, burn everything, leave nothing but ashes.

I opened a new encrypted chat window on my laptop. The cursor blinked, waiting.

I typed: "The leak is Wren. Don't trust her. I'll explain later."

My thumb hovered over the send button. Sasha would see the message. She'd know what to do. She'd help me contain the damage, protect the network, find a way forward.

But sending the message would tip my hand. Wren had access to the encrypted chat logs — she'd built the system herself. If she saw the message before I had a plan, she'd disappear. Or worse, she'd go to Victor Rhodes with everything she knew.

I stared at the unsent message for a long moment.

Then I closed the window.

I couldn't tip my hand yet. Wren was too dangerous to corner without a plan. And I didn't have a plan. Not yet.

But I would.

I looked at the death certificate still open on my screen. The signature that was a millimeter off. The proof that Priya had risked everything for me.

I owed it to her to survive this. To finish Victor Rhodes. To protect the network that had protected me.

Even if that meant destroying the person who had once been my closest ally.
